content:
Investigation came week after sighting in Mill Creek Watershed

PENDLETON — Someone — or something — lurked in the forests of Eastern Oregon in 1982 and left behind large footprints that prompted the U.S. Forest Service to investigate and make an official report.

Was it Bigfoot, the bulky, hairy cryptid people have reported in the Pacific Northwest for decades?

Not likely, according to the report the Forest Service released Oct. 15.

The report was one of three records about Bigfoot the federal agency released on its “Reading Room,” a webpage where the agency provides records it often receives Freedom of Information Act requests for.

The other two records are from Montana. One is a copy of a 2003 article in the Clark Fork Valley Press about the discovery of large humanlike footprints. The other is a six-page history from 1980 of the Petty Creek area that includes a personal account of a hunting party in 1949 coming upon elk entrails and a large set of bipedal tracks leading away. The four hunters followed the tracks, found they appeared to step over a log 3-feet in diameter and decided they “were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was.”

Wildlife biologist Rodney L. Johnson filed his Forest Service report on June 18, 1982, the day after he accompanied a group into the Mill Creek Watershed of the Blue Mountains to “investigate a reported find of ‘Bigfoot’ tracks in the Low Creek drainage.”

The Low Creek drainage is within the Mill Creek watershed inside the Umatilla National Forest and south of the Oregon-Washington border. Johnson’s seven-page report details the investigation into tracks at two locations in the drainage.

Site “A” was in the Low Ridge Trail approximately 1.5 miles above Mill Creek and contained six “identifiable tracks extending down the trail approximately 25 feet.” The second site was next to the Low Creek Trail, approximately 2.75 miles above Mill Creek and “contained approximately 18 prints over a distance of approximately 40 feet.”

The group took several photographs of the tracks and made two plaster casts of tracks at each site. Some prints were about 15 inches long.

There was a report of tracks at a third site, but the group didn’t examine that location due to the time of day and conclusions from the first two sites — that “something other than a 300 pound plus two footed being” made the tracks.

Johnson noted the stride of the tracks did not change with slope, and the stride “of all tracks observed was right at four (4) feet.” The tracks also did not sink deep into the mud.

“In fact, we were sinking in deeper with boots on at the same locations,” according to the report.

The tracks also did not connect to a trail and had a definite beginning and an end, unlike bear tracks the group observed. And the “toeprint markings” were clear and smooth instead of rough and calloused, plus there was no sign of heel or toe slippage on steep terrain.

Another telling sign, Johnson reported: At Site B, it was obvious the forest litter — needles and such — “had been displaced sideways from the track area in an unnatural manner.”

The examination also found the “foot” that made the tracks “may have been ‘rocked’ from side to side to leave the impression.

The observations added up to hoax footprints.

Johnson, however, gave credit to the Bigfoot track forger: “If the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail. The ‘print’ marks on the foot would have to be very hard to duplicate. They appear very natural.”

Johnson wrote whoever did this may have used a cast of a real foot to make the fake tracks.

The following month, Joel Hardin, with the U.S. Border Patrol in Bellingham, Washington, responded to Johnson’s report in a memo. Hardin was part of the team that investigated the tracks and is an expert tracker. After retiring from the Border Patrol he started Universal Tracking Services in Oregon.

“My opinion is that the tracks were a very clever attempt to perpetrate a hoax, involving your office or agency,” Hardin wrote, “in order to lend authenticity or credibility to the general public.”

Some type of soft plaster or rubber-coated foot may have been used to make the tracks, Hardin postulated, and the likely culprit would be “someone with normal access to the area, very knowledgeable and interested in ‘Bigfoot’ legends and stories; a person large enough to implant the track device sufficient to make the sign described and of which you have the evidence.”

Hardin added: “Trusting that this memo will suffice to close this ‘Bigfoot’ case.”

The investigation into the tracks came after Paul Freeman, a former U.S. Forest Service patrolman, reported on June 10, 1982, finding three sets of large footprints in the Mill Creek watershed of the Umatilla National Forest, according to The Spokesman-Review.

Freeman in 1994 made a video in the Blue Mountains of what he claimed was a bigfoot. Some Bigfoot investigators consider Freeman’s video to be authentic.

In addition to the trio of Bigfoot records, the reading room page includes six UFO reports, though none of them are from Oregon.
